newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's dollar set to soar on improved fiscal picture.
newsitem.headline: Canada's dollar set to soar on improved fiscal picture.

text.p: Despite falling interest rates, Canada's dollar hit a year high early Thursday and is set to soar against the U.S. dollar by year end, propelled by the nation's improving economic and fiscal fundamentals.
The Canadian dollar hit a peak of 74.13 cents (U.S.) in European trading early Thursday, but slid back to about 74.01 cents in North American trading on fears of a rate cut.
But economists said another Bank of Canada rate cut was unlikely to restrain the currency's rise.
"I think it will go to (75.47 cents) by the end of the year," said Andrew Spence, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Even Canadian foreign exchange traders, quick to price in rumours of an interest rate cut, seemed bullish.
"She's on a roll and I think we go stronger," said Eric Smail, foreign exchange salesman at Toronto-Dominion Bank.

Economists said reduced government spending and the emergence in the second quarter of a current account surplus had eliminated the need for monetary policy to be heavily weighted in favour of ever-deepening interest rate cuts.

"That re-calibration in monetary policies is only partially complete in that real interest rates have come down," Spence said. "Now it's the currency's turn, which means the currency should appreciate."

The Canadian dollar, which was trading at 74.83 cents in October 1995, has been restrained in the past year by a series of interest rate cuts in which the Bank of Canada's key lending rate fell to 4.0 percent from 6.63 percent.
Lower interest rates make Canadian denominated assets less attractive to investors.

Spence said longer-term structural adjustments to government spending in Canada led to the first current account surplus in 12 years and a shrinking foreign debt-to-GDP ratio, making a dollar rise likely.
"Which means that you don't have to have a heavily skewed mix of monetary conditions any more to counter the current account deficit," he said.

On Wednesday, Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said Canada's 1995/96 budget deficit came in $3 billion lower than originally projected and he pledged to lower it to 1 percent of gross domestic product by 1998/99 vs. a projected 3 percent for fiscal 1996/97 ending March 31.
He said the government anticipated the nation's total debt-to-GDP ratio would begin declining after 1997-98 and that he expected the government to balance the budget.

Bank of Canada Gov. Gordon Thiessen said Wednesday that the central bank's low-inflation monetary policy had created room for the currency to rise 1.5 percent annually without hurting Canada's export competitiveness.
Thiessen said that a dollar rise was possible because of the 1.5 percentage point inflation gap between Canada and the United States, Canada's main trading partner.
"At the very least, the currency can increase at the rate of 1.5 percent a year without affecting the competitiveness of our exports, Thiessen told reporters after a speech.
